slides.body: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery.
In video 127 you carried one change through the fork workflow.
You sync the fork's main, update your branch once by rebase and once by merge, answer a review round, and see what a squash merge does to the question "is my branch merged?".
A note on layers, which the chapter makes at its start: branches, tags, merges and rebases are Git.
Here's what you'll walk away with.

params.title: Merged by content, not by ancestry

slides.direction: Later, after the squash merge in the demo, the root-cause box of section 27.3.
slides.text:
Observed behavior : after a squash merge, "is my branch merged?" gets three different answers.
Git state         : upstream main has one new commit, 16e9e75. Your branch tip is 147ed67.
                    147ed67 is not an ancestor of 16e9e75.
Mechanism         : "merged" in Git means "reachable from". git merge-base --is-ancestor and
                    git branch --merged both test reachability, and a squash creates a commit
                    with one parent and no link to your commits.
Root cause        : the merge method discarded the ancestry and kept the content.
Why Git does this : a commit's parents are part of its ID. Git cannot record "these commits were
                    folded into that one" without a second parent, and a second parent is
                    exactly what a squash omits.
Correct fix       : test content, not ancestry: an empty "git diff main <branch>" here, or the
                    merge-tree comparison of Lab 34.1 when main has moved further.
Prevention        : delete the branch right after the merge, on the fork and locally, and never
                    reuse it. Chapter 17, section 17.12 shows what reuse does to the next pull request.

slides.body: Then go back to the contributor's clone, sync main with the fast-forward relay, and delete the branch in both places.
Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Committing on the fork's main. Root cause: the fork's default branch is treated as a working branch, so it stops being a copy of upstream and can no longer be fast-forwarded.
Starting the topic branch from the fork's main instead of upstream/main. Root cause: nothing updates the fork for you, so its main is an old commit and the pull request starts behind.
Asking "is it merged?" with an ancestry test after a squash merge. Root cause: the merge method discarded the ancestry and kept the content.
Force-pushing over a review in progress. Root cause: the reviewer's comments are anchored to commits that the rebase replaced, so their work has to be redone.
Pushing guesses at a red check on a fork pull request. Root cause: workflows from forks run without the project's secrets, so a job that needs one fails whatever the code does.

slides.body: Let's land this in your own words.

items: The fork workflow has three repositories and two remotes; you fetch from upstream and push to origin.
The fork's main is a relay that only fast-forwards; git merge --ff-only upstream/main is both the sync and the guard.
A topic branch is updated by rebase, which needs a forced push with a lease, or by merge, which needs a plain push and leaves a merge commit.
After a squash merge the branch is not merged by ancestry; test content, then delete the branch and never reuse it.
A maintainer's scarce resource is attention: contribution guide first, issue first, one logical change, say what you tested.

slides.body: Read sections 27.1 to 27.4.
Today you kept a fork in step with a moving project, and you sat in the maintainer's chair.

beats.text: A team that depends on an open-source gateway finds a bug, fixes it in an afternoon and opens a pull request. Three weeks later nothing has happened. Meanwhile the project's main has moved, the pull request shows a conflict, and the engineer's fork says it is "two commits ahead, forty behind". Nobody on the team can say how the fork got ahead of a project they never had write access to.
beats.tele: A team that depends on an open-source gateway finds a bug, fixes it in an afternoon and opens a pull request. Three weeks later nothing has happened. Meanwhile the project's `main` has moved, the pull request shows a conflict, and the engineer's fork says it is "two commits ahead, forty behind". Nobody on the team can say how the fork got ahead of a project they never had write access to.

beats.text: The first is the fork's default branch. It should be an exact copy of the project's main. A strong answer explains both numbers from the graph: what "ahead" means for a branch that should only relay, and why "behind" is the normal state of a fork nobody synced. It names the read-only command that shows the two counts. It then repairs in an order that can't lose work: the two commits get a name before main is moved. And it says what would have stopped the mistake at the moment it was made, which is one option on one command you saw today.

beats.text: The fork workflow has three repositories and two remotes; you fetch from upstream and push to origin.
beats.tele: The fork workflow has three repositories and two remotes; you fetch from `upstream` and push to `origin`.

beats.text: The fork's main is a relay that only fast-forwards; git merge --ff-only upstream/main is both the sync and the guard.
beats.tele: The fork's `main` is a relay that only fast-forwards; `git merge --ff-only upstream/main` is both the sync and the guard.

beats.text: A topic branch is updated by rebase, which needs a forced push with a lease, or by merge, which needs a plain push and leaves a merge commit.
beats.tele: A topic branch is updated by rebase, which needs a forced push with a lease, or by merge, which needs a plain push and leaves a merge commit.

beats.text: After a squash merge the branch is not merged by ancestry; test content, then delete the branch and never reuse it.
